traveler: Gilles de Montmorency-Laval, baron de Rais, Marshal of France
title: The Marshal's Road: from the Loire of Joan of Arc to the gibbets of Nantes
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Champtocé-sur-Loire, birth in the castle chapel
stops.date_confidence: disputed: estimates run from 1396 to 1406, with September or October 1404 and 1405 most often cited; no birth record survives and the disagreement is not resolvable from the sources reached
stops.campa: In the castle above the north bank of the Loire a son is born to Guy de Rais and Marie de Craon, and is baptised in the chapel within the walls. He is heir on both sides: Rais and Laval from his father, Craon and Champtocé from his mother, a fortune scattered across Brittany, Anjou, Poitou, Maine, and Angoumois. The chapel where the water touches him stands today in ruin and is listed as a monument historique in 1926. The walls that will be named in the indictment read against him thirty-five years on are the walls he is carried through as an infant.
suggested_refs: The ruined keep and castle chapel of Champtocé-sur-Loire, listed monument historique 16 June 1926

stops.name: Machecoul, the death of Guy de Rais
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1415; the day is not given in the sources reached
stops.campa: Guy de Rais dies at Machecoul in October, and the two boys, Gilles and his younger brother René, pass into the guardianship of their maternal grandfather Jean de Craon, lord of Champtocé and Ingrandes. Craon runs the wardship as an estate operation: two heirs, two marriages to be sold, two fortunes to be gathered into one. Gilles is ten or eleven. In the same month, three hundred miles to the north, the French chivalry is destroyed at Agincourt. Gilles will spend his twenties in the war that runs on from that field.
suggested_refs: The Château de Machecoul, head of the barony of Retz, now ruined

stops.name: Champtoceaux, the siege in the Breton civil war
stops.date_confidence: the siege ran May to July 1420 and ended in capitulation on 5 July; the February to May range given in the pool is wrong, and Gilles's personal presence is reconstruction, not attestation
stops.campa: Marguerite de Clisson seizes Duke Jean V of Brittany in February and holds him prisoner; the loyalist army answers by laying siege to her fortress above the Loire at Champtoceaux, and takes its capitulation with the honours of war on the fifth of July. Gilles is fifteen or sixteen, riding under his grandfather's banner in what his biographers count as the first campaign of a soldier's career. Nothing in the local record of the siege names him. He is placed here by the men who wrote his life, not by the men who were at the walls.
suggested_refs: The promontory fortress of Champtoceaux, slighted after the 1420 siege

stops.name: Chalonnes-sur-Loire, the marriage to Catherine de Thouars
stops.date_confidence: sources contradict: one gives an abduction and marriage in 1420 with papal validation in 1422 after her father's death, another gives the church ceremony itself on 26 June 1422; both may describe different acts, and the contradiction is left open
stops.campa: Jean de Craon wants the Thouars inheritance and does not wait for a dispensation. Gilles carries off his cousin Catherine de Thouars and marries her without the church's leave, which brings him Tiffauges and Pouzauges and the Poitevin lands attached to them. The union is solemnized afterwards at Chalonnes and the irregularity is papered over. He is seventeen or eighteen and among the richest men in France. The two castles that arrive with his wife will both be named in the bill of articles read against him at Nantes eighteen years later.
suggested_refs: The Thouars and Pouzauges inheritance, brought to Rais by the marriage of 1420 or 1422
sources: medievalmatt.substack.com, 'Have You Heard of Gilles de Rais?'

stops.name: Le Mans, raiding the garrisons of Maine
stops.date_confidence: 1427 is the year English Wikipedia gives for the start of active service; French Wikipedia dates his service from about 1420, so the beginning is not fixed
stops.campa: Gilles takes the field on the Maine frontier with the captain Ambroise de Loré, riding against the English garrisons that hold the country between the Sarthe and the Loire. It is the ordinary war of the period: surprise, ambush, the storming of small places, ransom, the burning of what cannot be carried. He is good at it, and he is rich enough to raise and pay men out of his own coffers for as long as a season lasts. By the time a peasant girl reaches the court at Chinon he is a captain the crown can call on and does not have to fund.
suggested_refs: The Maine frontier campaigns of Ambroise de Loré, 1427 to 1429

stops.name: Blois, the convoy for the relief of Orléans
stops.date_confidence: the pool's 25 April is two or three days early; the relief convoy left Blois on 27 or 28 April 1429
stops.campa: The relief force for Orléans musters at Blois: victual carts, herded cattle, the captains of France, La Hire, and a girl in white harness whom the king has sent with them. Gilles de Rais is among the noble captains gathered here and rides out with the convoy. The written accounts of the muster name the marshals present without listing him by name, though he rides among them. From this week until the anointing at Reims eleven weeks later, he is at every place she is remembered for.
suggested_refs: The muster of the Orléans relief convoy at Blois, April 1429

stops.name: Orléans, the relief force enters by the Burgundy gate
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Joan enters the besieged city on the twenty-ninth with Dunois at her side and the townspeople pressing so close about the horse that a torch sets her banner alight. The convoy and its captains follow over the next days as the boats are worked upriver past the English bastilles. Gilles commands troops in this force. He is twenty-four or twenty-five, a Breton baron who has never seen the French side win anything larger than a raid. Orléans is the first siege of his life that gets lifted.
suggested_refs: The Burgundy gate of Orléans, by which the relief entered on 29 April 1429
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json (Orléans, entry by the Burgundy gate)

stops.name: Bastille Saint-Loup, the first bastille stormed
stops.date_confidence: 4 May 1429, launched at midday; the 6 May carried in the Wikipedia article on Gilles de Rais is an error, since 6 May was the assault on Saint-Jean-le-Blanc and Les Augustins
stops.campa: At midday Dunois throws the garrison at the English earthwork of Saint-Loup, east of the walls, and Joan rides out to it when she hears the noise of the fighting. The bastille is carried and burned and its defenders killed or taken. Gilles fights in this assault, the first outright French success of the siege and the proof to the men inside the city that the ring of forts can be broken at all. The southern bastilles go two days later and the bridge fort the day after that.
suggested_refs: The site of the bastille Saint-Loup, east of Orléans

stops.name: Les Tourelles, the bridge-fort carried
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The fortified bridgehead on the south bank is the last and hardest of the English works, and the assault on it runs from dawn until dark. Joan takes an arrow above the breast, has it drawn out, and is back at the ditch before evening; the fort falls with its commander drowned in the Loire under the weight of his armour. Gilles fights here. Six years later he will pay for this day to be reenacted in this city by hundreds of costumed men, and the bill for it will be among the things that ruin him.
suggested_refs: The Tourelles bridgehead on the south bank of the Loire at Orléans

stops.name: Orléans, the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the morning of the eighth the English burn their camps and draw up in order of battle outside the walls; the French come out, hear mass in the open field facing them, and let them march away unfought. The siege of seven months is over. Gilles rides in the procession through a city that votes its yearly commemoration of the deliverance and keeps it, unbroken, into the present century. The commemoration remembers Joan and the townspeople of Orléans. It does not remember him.
suggested_refs: The Fêtes johanniques of Orléans, kept every 8 May since 1430

segments.name: The Week of Victories and the Anointing

stops.name: Jargeau, the storming of the town
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Loire campaign opens against Suffolk's garrison at Jargeau upstream. The town is bombarded through the night, then taken by escalade in a single afternoon of savage close work at the ladders; Suffolk surrenders and the English dead are counted in the hundreds. Gilles takes part in the assault, and Joan is knocked off a ladder by a stone that splits her helmet. Alençon commands and La Hire and Dunois are in the line. The army that fought its way into Orléans six weeks ago is now the army doing the besieging.
suggested_refs: The walls of Jargeau, stormed 12 June 1429

stops.name: Meung-sur-Loire, the bridge taken
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The army does not stop to reduce the town or the castle; it storms the bridge fortress at Meung, puts a garrison in it, and moves on downstream the same day, cutting the English line along the river in half. Gilles de Rais is named among the captains of this force. Three river crossings pass into French hands in four days, and the English field army under Fastolf, marching south to relieve them, is still a day's ride off and will arrive to find the crossings already lost.
suggested_refs: The bridge fortress of Meung-sur-Loire, taken 15 June 1429

stops.name: Beaugency, the surrender
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Beaugency's garrison, cut off from Meung and watching for a relief that does not come, treats for terms and marches out under safe conduct. Richemont, Constable of France and out of favour at court, brings up his Breton companies uninvited and is taken into the army against the king's wishes because nobody will turn away that many lances. Gilles rides in the same force, a Breton among Bretons, under a constable his own king has forbidden the court to receive.
suggested_refs: The keep of Beaugency, surrendered 16 June 1429

stops.name: Patay, the English broken in the field
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The English archers are caught in the open country north of the Loire before their stakes are planted, by French cavalry riding at them out of the scrub after a startled stag gives away the position. The line breaks in minutes. Talbot is taken prisoner, Fastolf rides off the field and loses his Garter for it, and two thousand English dead are left in the fields toward Patay. Gilles fights in the charge. It is fourteen years since Agincourt and the road to Reims now lies open.
suggested_refs: The field of Patay, 18 June 1429

stops.name: Reims, marshal of France at the coronation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the marshalcy and the coronation; the identification of Gilles as one of the four knights who escorted the Sainte Ampoule is tradition rather than document, and the corpus's joan_of_arc file names the four without naming them
stops.campa: Charles VII is anointed with the oil of the Sainte Ampoule in the cathedral, Joan standing near the altar with her standard because, she says, it had borne the pain and deserved the honour. Gilles de Rais is raised to Marshal of France on the day, and rides armed into the church among the lords escorting the holy ampulla to the altar. He is twenty-four or so and holds, from this morning, the highest military rank the kingdom can give a man. It is the summit of his life. He has eleven years left.
suggested_refs: The Sainte Ampoule and the coronation of Charles VII at Reims, 17 July 1429
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json (Reims, the coronation of Charles VII)

segments.name: The March on Paris and the Last Campaigns

stops.name: Montépilloy, the skirmish before Senlis
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Bedford brings the English army out of Paris and takes ground near Senlis; the two hosts face each other across ditches and hedges the whole of a hot August day without either committing to the attack. Joan rides up to the palisade and strikes it with her standard, inviting a battle that does not come, and by evening both armies withdraw. Gilles is present at this inconclusive day. The advance on Paris stops here and does not get going again for three weeks, and neither army has the strength to push the other off the ground.
suggested_refs: The field of Montépilloy, near Senlis, 15 August 1429

stops.name: Paris, the assault on the Porte Saint-Honoré
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the feast of the Nativity of the Virgin the army attacks the northwest wall of Paris. Joan stands in the dry ditch sounding the depth of the wet one with a lance and calls on the city to surrender for the love of Jesus; a crossbow bolt goes through her thigh and she has to be carried away after dark, still refusing to withdraw. Gilles stands beside her in the assault. The attack fails, and within days the king orders the army broken up and sends its captains home.
suggested_refs: The Porte Saint-Honoré, where Joan was wounded on 8 September 1429
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json (Paris, the assault on the Porte Saint-Honoré)

stops.name: Lagny-sur-Marne, the siege lifted
stops.date_confidence: 1432; the month is given as August by one lens only and is not fixed in the sources reached
stops.campa: Three years after Paris, Gilles helps raise the English siege of Lagny on the Marne, an action his biographers count among the best pieces of soldiering he ever did. Joan of Arc had fought at this town herself in the spring of 1430, and had been burned at Rouen fourteen months before this relief. It is close to the last thing Gilles does in the field. After Lagny he is in his own castles, spending his own money. He is twenty-seven, and his grandfather has three months left to live.
suggested_refs: The relief of Lagny-sur-Marne, 1432, his last recorded feat of arms

stops.name: Champtocé, the death of Jean de Craon
stops.date_confidence: November 1432; the day is not given in the sources reached
stops.campa: The grandfather who raised him, married him off, and held the family lands together for seventeen years dies in November, and the whole inherited weight of Craon and Champtocé comes onto Gilles at once. He is twenty-seven or so and answerable to nobody living. Tradition holds that the old man at the end passed him over for the sword and the treasure of the house and left them to his younger brother René instead. From this winter the estate begins to be sold, and the indictment of 1440 will date the killing of children from about this time.
suggested_refs: The Craon inheritance, entered in November 1432

stops.name: Machecoul, the children begin to disappear
stops.date_confidence: the onset is disputed: the indictment-derived chronology gives about 1432, other accounts late 1433; nothing contemporary fixes it and neither figure is adopted here
stops.campa: Children go missing from the villages around Machecoul. Boys mostly, between eight and twelve: beggars fed at the gate, herdboys, apprentices offered a place in a great lord's household on terms no poor family refuses. The parents ask at the castle and are told nothing. Machecoul is the head of the barony of Retz and the house named more often than any other in the bill of articles eight years later. The ecclesiastical court will count a hundred and forty victims. His own servants, questioned separately, will say the number could not be counted.
stops.quote: he took and had others take so many children that he could not determine with certitude the number whom he'd killed
stops.quote_source: Confession of Gilles de Rais before the ecclesiastical tribunal at Nantes, 22 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 195-203, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The 49 articles of the 1440 indictment, which name Machecoul first among the houses
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Chinon, the fall of Georges de La Trémoille
stops.date_confidence: June 1433; the day is not given in the sources reached
stops.campa: Gilles's kinsman and patron, the grand chamberlain Georges de La Trémoille, who has run Charles VII and the war for six years, is ambushed by a court faction, stabbed, and driven from power. Gilles loses at a stroke the man who made his career and guarded his interests at court. His daughter Marie is born the same year, his only child. He does not appear again in royal service. He keeps the title of marshal and nothing that came with it, and nobody at court now has a reason to shield a Breton baron who is spending faster than he earns.
suggested_refs: The 1433 coup against Georges de La Trémoille at the court of Charles VII
sources: joan_of_arc.journey.json (Chinon, the recognition of the Dauphin)

stops.name: Orléans, the Mystère du siège d'Orléans
stops.date_confidence: 1435; the run of performances is not precisely dated in the sources reached, and the whole enterprise is reported as tradition rather than as document
stops.campa: He commissions and pays for a theatrical reconstruction of the siege he fought in six years before, a mystery play of some twenty thousand lines with five hundred speaking parts, staged in the city itself. The costumes are made new for every performance and given away afterwards. Food and hippocras are free to anyone who comes, for as many days as the town will watch. He watches his own best week performed back to him and pays for it by selling land. His family will name the Mystère among the things that ruined him.
suggested_refs: The Mystère du siège d'Orléans, financed by Rais at Orléans in 1435

stops.name: Ingrandes, the lands sold and the king's edict
stops.date_confidence: July 1435 for the royal edict; the sales run from about 1435 to 1437, and the place where the letters were issued is not named in the sources reached
stops.campa: Seigneurie by seigneurie the inheritance goes: Ingrandes and the other Angevin lordships, sold or mortgaged to Breton and Angevin buyers at whatever they will pay on the day. The family petitions the crown, and in July Charles VII issues letters forbidding Gilles to alienate any more of his estates and warning his subjects against buying from him. Duke Jean V of Brittany declines to publish the edict in his own duchy and goes on buying. A marshal of France is forbidden by his own king to sell his own land.
suggested_refs: The royal letters of July 1435 restraining Rais from selling his estates

stops.name: Machecoul, the chapel of the Holy Innocents
stops.date_confidence: about 1435 to 1436; the foundation is not precisely dated in the sources reached and rests on a single chronology
stops.campa: He founds and endows a collegiate chapel at Machecoul under the title of the Holy Innocents, with a dean, canons, choirboys, and vestments of a magnificence the bishop of Nantes objects to. The Innocents are the children of Bethlehem killed by Herod's soldiers, the feast the church keeps every December in their memory. Gilles dedicates his chapel to them, on the ground where, by the testimony his own servants give in 1440, children are being killed while the canons sing the hours.
stops.quote: They found forty-six that were put into coffers and transported to Machecoul and burned
stops.quote_source: Confession of Etienne Corrillaut, called Poitou, Nantes, October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 279-282, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The collegiate chapel of the Holy Innocents at Machecoul, founded and endowed by Rais
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Poitou
jesus.journey.json (Bethlehem, the Massacre of the Innocents)

stops.name: Château de Pouzauges, the Thouars castle
stops.date_confidence: held from 1420 or 1422; no date attaches to the acts named here beyond the indictment's span of 1432 to 1440
stops.campa: Pouzauges came with Catherine de Thouars and is now his wife's residence, its round keep standing over the bocage of the Vendée. It is named among the houses of the barony where children are brought in and are not seen again. Catherine and their daughter Marie live apart from him through most of these years. The wife is never charged, never questioned in the surviving record, and nothing she said has come down; the sources reached name her only as an heiress and, after October 1440, as a widow who remarries within the year.
stops.quote: he sat on their bellies and delighted in watching them die thus
stops.quote_source: Confession of Gilles de Rais before the ecclesiastical tribunal at Nantes, 22 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 195-203, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The round keep of the Château de Pouzauges, Vendée
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: La Roche-Bernard, the children reported missing
stops.date_confidence: no year is fixed; the testimony belongs to the span of disappearances running from about 1432 to 1440
stops.campa: The rumour travels outward along the roads of the duchy. At La Roche-Bernard on the Vilaine, sixty miles from Machecoul, a child is taken into the marshal's service and does not come home, and the mother's complaint is entered in the record of 1440 with dozens like it. The parents of the missing have been talking to one another for years. Nobody in Brittany with the power to act has wanted to hear a marshal of France accused, and when the accusation finally arrives it comes attached to an entirely different crime.
suggested_refs: The depositions of parents from the Breton parishes, gathered September 1440
sources: famous-trials.com, transcriptions of the 1440 trial documents

stops.name: Hôtel de la Suze, Nantes
stops.date_confidence: no date attaches; the house is named in the 1440 indictment among those used across the whole span from 1432 to 1440
stops.campa: His townhouse in Nantes, the Hôtel de la Suze, is named in the indictment beside Champtocé, Machecoul, and Tiffauges. The building is gone and no reachable source fixes where it stood beyond the old town. In a city of twelve or fifteen thousand souls, with the ducal castle a few streets off and the cathedral works going up, the household comes and goes and the servants Henriet Griart and Poitou carry in and out whatever has to be carried. The court will hear how the bodies were burned and the ashes put out of the way.
stops.quote: he saw two dead children in the room of the said Lord, who wanted to kill him
stops.quote_source: Confession of Etienne Corrillaut, called Poitou, Nantes, October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 279-282, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The vanished Hôtel de la Suze in the old town of Nantes
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Poitou
famous-trials.com, transcription of the Indictment of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Château de Tiffauges, the furnace
stops.date_confidence: the alchemical work at Tiffauges is dated by trial testimony to the years around 1438 and 1439; the tradition is firmer than the dating
stops.campa: Ruined and unable to stop spending, he turns to men who say they can make gold. Priests, goldsmiths, and conjurors pass through Tiffauges, are lodged, fed, paid, and dismissed when the furnace gives them nothing. The work runs in a lower room kept locked: powders, an athanor, circles drawn on the floor, invocations of a demon called Barron who is asked for knowledge, riches, and power. Barron never appears and the debts go on growing. He keeps at it because the alternative is to sell the last of the land his grandfather gathered.
stops.quote: there was no man alive who could ever understand what he had done, and it was because of his planet
stops.quote_source: Confession of Henriet Griart, Nantes, October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 275-279, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The Château de Tiffauges above the Sèvre Nantaise, called locally the castle of Barbe-Bleue
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Henriet

stops.name: Tiffauges, the arrival of François Prelati
stops.date_confidence: the precise date of 14 May 1439 appears in one chronology and is corroborated by nothing else reached; treat it as reconstruction
stops.campa: A young Tuscan cleric from Montecatini in the diocese of Lucca, who calls himself François de Montcatin, is brought to Tiffauges and installed as the household's conjuror. Prelati is charming, plausible, about twenty-two, and claims a familiar spirit of his own. He works in the tower, shows bruises he says the demon gave him, and promises gold that never comes. Gilles believes him for a year and a half. At Nantes in 1440 Prelati will testify against him, weep with him at the parting, and be sentenced to prison rather than to the fire.
suggested_refs: The testimony of François Prelati at the Nantes trial, October 1440

stops.name: Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte, the church broken open
stops.date_confidence: attested and commemorated on a plaque in the church; the ducal recapture that follows is dated 24 August 1440 by a single narrative source that was unreachable at verification
stops.campa: He has sold the castle of Saint-Étienne to Geoffroy Le Ferron, treasurer of Brittany, and he wants it back. On Whitsunday, during high mass, Gilles comes into the parish church with armed men, seizes the treasurer's brother Jean Le Ferron at the altar, beats him, and takes the castle by force. Le Ferron is a tonsured clerk and the castle stands under ducal protection. In August the duke's men retake it and free him. The bishop of Nantes now has jurisdiction over a marshal of France, and begins to ask what else is said about him.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque in the church of Saint-Étienne-de-Mer-Morte recording the seizure of Jean Le Ferron

stops.name: Machecoul, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Officers of Duke Jean V come to Machecoul on the fifteenth of September and arrest Gilles de Rais together with his servants Henriet Griart and Etienne Corrillaut, called Poitou. He does not resist. He has men in his pay and uses none of them. The summons already joins the assault on Le Ferron to the murder of children, so he knows before he mounts what he is being taken for. They ride him up the road to Nantes, to the ducal castle whose new tower he will not leave alive.
suggested_refs: The ducal summons of September 1440, joining the Le Ferron affair to the murder of children

stops.name: Nantes, the inquest and the innkeepers' testimony
stops.date_confidence: 18 September 1440 for the deposition document; the secular inquest opens in the same week
stops.campa: The secular inquest opens and the parents come in to be heard. Women who keep an inn at Machecoul describe how Poitou bought a boy from his mother, Peronne Loessart, for a place in the lord's household and a payment of money, and they repeat what the lord said when the child was brought before him. The mother never saw the boy again. Depositions of this kind pile up through September, one household at a time, until the ecclesiastical court has enough of them to draw a bill of articles.
stops.quote: the child was as beautiful as an angel
stops.quote_source: Testimony concerning a missing child, Nantes, 18 September 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 253-255, trans. Richard Robinson; reported by the innkeeper witnesses, not spoken by Peronne Loessart
suggested_refs: The September 1440 depositions of the parents of missing children, Nantes
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of Testimony concerning a missing child

stops.name: Château des ducs de Bretagne, the indictment read
stops.date_confidence: 13 October 1440 for the bill of forty-nine articles; a first indictment in general terms was laid on 13 September, and the pool's dating of the articles to September conflates the two
stops.campa: In the upper hall of the Tour Neuve the promoter reads out the bill of forty-nine articles: heresy, apostasy, the invocation of demons, sodomy, and the murder of children, whom the ecclesiastical court numbers at a hundred and forty. Gilles calls the judges simoniacs and scoundrels and refuses to answer them, and is excommunicated on the spot for contumacy. Three days later he asks to be heard again, apologises to the court, and asks for the excommunication to be lifted. From that hour he cooperates with the men who will burn him.
stops.quote: took, killed, cut the throats of many children, boys and girls
stops.quote_source: Indictment of Gilles de Rais, Article XV, Nantes, 13 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 169-180, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The Tour Neuve of the Château des ducs de Bretagne, courtroom of the ecclesiastical trial
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Indictment of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Nantes, the servants questioned
stops.date_confidence: the confessions of Henriet and Poitou are taken in the second half of October 1440; the sources reached give the month only, so the day is placed
stops.campa: Henriet Griart and Poitou are questioned apart from their master and apart from each other, and their accounts agree. They name the castles, the rooms, the method, the burning of the bodies, and the numbers as far as either of them can count. Both have served him for years. Both were themselves taken into the household as boys and kept. Everything the court does afterwards rests on these two statements and on what Gilles says himself five days later. Both men will hang beside him.
stops.quote: The said Lord took greater pleasure in cutting their throats or watching their throats be cut than in knowing them carnally.
stops.quote_source: Confession of Henriet Griart, Nantes, October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 275-279, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The parallel confessions of Henriet Griart and Etienne Corrillaut, Nantes, October 1440
sources: famous-trials.com, transcriptions of the Confessions of Henriet and Poitou

stops.name: The Tour Neuve, the confession
stops.date_confidence: the in-court confession is of 22 October 1440; 21 October was the separate out-of-court interrogation, and the pool dated the courtroom document to the wrong day
stops.campa: Torture is ordered and shown to him, and he asks that it be deferred and offers to tell everything freely instead. On the twenty-first he is examined out of court; on the twenty-second he confesses in open session, at length, unpressed, and asks the parents of the children to forgive him. The court that convened to try a heretic hears a marshal of France describe what he did in his own castles and how much he enjoyed doing it. He asks that his confession be published in French, so that the common people can hear it.
stops.quote: humbly and tearfully implored the mercy and pardon of His Creator
stops.quote_source: Confession of Gilles de Rais, Nantes, 22 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 195-203, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The in-court confession of 22 October 1440, published in French at his own request
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Confession of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Nantes, the two courts sentence him
stops.date_confidence: attested for both ecclesiastical sentences; the secular sentence is known from the narrative accounts and does not appear in the surviving sentencing document
stops.campa: The ecclesiastical court pronounces twice in the same session, once for apostasy and the invocation of demons, once for sodomy on children of both sexes, and then reconciles him to the church after he asks for absolution and receives it. The secular court sitting at the fortress of Le Bouffay under Pierre de l'Hôpital, president of Brittany, sentences him to be hanged and burned for the murders. Two jurisdictions have run in parallel for a fortnight, the church for heresy and the duke for killing, and they arrive on the same day.
stops.quote: Gilles de Rais, present before us in trial, are found guilty of perfidious apostasy as well as of the dreadful invocation of demons
stops.quote_source: Sentencing of Gilles de Rais, ecclesiastical court, Nantes, 25 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 207-208, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: The fortress of Le Bouffay at Nantes, seat of the ducal secular court
sources: famous-trials.com, transcription of the Sentencing of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Île de la Grande Biesse, the three gibbets
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date and the hanging; the two lenses give coordinates 400 metres apart for a meadow on an island that no longer exists, and the contradiction is not resolved
stops.campa: In a meadow on an island in the Loire beyond the city, three gibbets stand over three prepared pyres, the tallest of them in the middle. Gilles de Rais is hanged first, before eleven in the morning, with Henriet and Poitou after him, and the fires are lit under all three. A crowd fills the meadow, and in it stand the parents of children who did not come back. The fire is drawn off his body before it is consumed, by noblewomen who have come to the ground for exactly that purpose and are permitted to take it.
stops.quote: We have sinned, all three of us, but as soon as our souls depart our bodies we shall all see God in His glory in Heaven
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Gilles de Rais at the scaffold, 26 October 1440; carried in the narrative accounts of the trial and absent from the primary confession and sentencing documents, so a reconstruction
suggested_refs: The Île de la Grande Biesse, execution ground of 26 October 1440, since filled in and built over
sources: famous-trials.com, narrative account of the trial (HTTP 404 at verification)

stops.name: Notre-Dame des Carmes, the burial
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial and the church; the two lenses give coordinates 360 metres apart for the vanished convent and neither figure is sourced
stops.campa: The same evening the body is carried into the Carmelite church of Nantes and buried near the tombs of the dukes of Brittany, with the honours owed a penitent who died reconciled to the church. Four women of rank claim it from the pyre and see the thing done. He is thirty-five or thirty-six. The two servants burn to ash in the meadow and are scattered; the marshal of France goes into consecrated ground beneath a monument, and the children whose parents stood in the crowd have no graves at all.
suggested_refs: The vanished convent church of Notre-Dame des Carmes, Nantes, burial place of Gilles de Rais
sources: famous-trials.com, narrative account of the trial (HTTP 404 at verification)

stops.name: Paris, La Barbe bleue
stops.date_confidence: 1697 for Perrault's collection; the identification of Gilles de Rais with Bluebeard is not traced earlier than the nineteenth century and modern scholarship treats it as speculative
stops.campa: Charles Perrault publishes Histoires ou contes du temps passé, and in it a tale about a rich lord with a blue beard, a forbidden room, and a line of wives who do not come out of it. Two centuries later, folk tradition and then popular history make Gilles de Rais the original. Nothing shows that Perrault knew anything about him, and the scholars who work on the trial record say so plainly. The identification travels anyway, and for most readers now it is the only thing they know about the marshal.
suggested_refs: Charles Perrault, Histoires ou contes du temps passé (1697), 'La Barbe bleue'

stops.name: Chaussée de la Madeleine, Notre-Dame-de-Crée-Lait
stops.date_confidence: 1867 for the disappearance of the monument; its erection is not dated in the sources reached, and the whole entry rests on one site that returned HTTP 404 at verification
stops.campa: Near the execution ground an expiatory monument stands for centuries, called Notre-Dame-de-Crée-Lait, and pregnant women and nursing mothers come to it to ask for milk. The Carmelite church and the tomb inside it are destroyed in the Revolution and nothing of the monument over his grave survives in place. The Crée-Lait itself disappears in 1867 and fragments of it are kept at the Musée Dobrée. The island where the gibbets stood has been filled in and built over, and the quarter keeps the name of the meadow.
suggested_refs: Fragments of the Notre-Dame-de-Crée-Lait monument, Musée Dobrée, Nantes
sources: patrimonia.nantes.fr (HTTP 404 at verification; sole source for this entry)

stops.name: Paris, Là-bas
stops.date_confidence: serialised from 15 February 1891 in L'Écho de Paris and issued in book form that April
stops.campa: Joris-Karl Huysmans serialises Là-bas in L'Écho de Paris. Its protagonist Durtal is writing a life of Gilles de Rais and reads himself out of the fifteenth century straight into the satanism of contemporary Paris. The novel treats the marshal as a case to be studied, and it is the book through which the Decadents, and after them nearly everyone else, come to him. Most of what gets written about Gilles de Rais over the next hundred years begins here rather than in the archive at Nantes.
suggested_refs: Joris-Karl Huysmans, Là-bas (1891), serialised in L'Écho de Paris

stops.name: Paris, the trial documents printed
stops.date_confidence: 1965 for the Pauvert edition; the English translation by Richard Robinson is dated 1991 by Open Library and 2004 by booksellers, and that contradiction is left open
stops.campa: Georges Bataille publishes Le Procès de Gilles de Rais with J.-J. Pauvert: the Latin minutes of the ecclesiastical court rendered into French by Pierre Klossowski, the whole dossier framed by an essay of his own. Amok Books later brings out an English version translated by Richard Robinson. For the first time the bill of articles, the confessions of the two servants, the words Gilles spoke in the Tour Neuve, and the sentences can be read straight through by anyone who wants to, with no novelist standing in between.
stops.quote: a heretic, a relapsed heretic, a magician, a sodomite, a conjuror of evil spirits
stops.quote_source: Indictment of Gilles de Rais, Article XLV, Nantes, 13 October 1440, in Georges Bataille, The Trial of Gilles de Rais (Amok Books), pp. 169-180, trans. Richard Robinson
suggested_refs: Georges Bataille, Le Procès de Gilles de Rais (J.-J. Pauvert, 1965), Latin minutes translated by Pierre Klossowski
sources: Open Library catalogue entry for Bataille, Le Procès de Gilles de Rais
famous-trials.com, transcription of the Indictment of Gilles de Rais

stops.name: Nantes, the mock rehabilitation
stops.date_confidence: 1992 for the staged trial and for Prouteau's book; the earlier rehabilitation essay by Salomon Reinach, who died in 1932, is undated in the sources reached and no date is printed here
stops.campa: A rehabilitation trial is staged and Gilles de Rais is declared innocent, the church and the duke of Brittany cast as the framers who wanted his land. Gilbert Prouteau, who organised it and published Gilles de Rais ou la Gueule du loup the same year, called the proceeding a monumental farce mounted with high-class accomplices, and was still laughing about it years afterward. The medievalists who work on the record, Jacques Chiffoleau and Claude Gauvard among them, read the trial as a trial and do not exonerate him.
suggested_refs: Gilbert Prouteau, Gilles de Rais ou la Gueule du loup (Éditions du Rocher, 1992)

stops.name: Tiffauges, the ruins
stops.date_confidence: present day
stops.campa: The keep at Tiffauges stands roofless above the Sèvre, and the walls at Champtocé and Machecoul stand roofless too, all three open to anyone who pays at the gate. There is no statue of Gilles de Rais: not at Nantes, not at Orléans, not on the Loire, in a country that has put Joan of Arc on horseback in a thousand towns and in the town where he was hanged. What is left of him is three ruins, a lost tomb, a vanished votive stone, and a children's story about a man with a blue beard.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Tiffauges, Champtocé, and Machecoul, the three castles named in the indictment
